opening.headline: Deployment unit management reduces confusion caused by different prompt versions across development, staging, and operations.
body: With the same app, prompt versions differ across environments, leading to strange responses from operations teams, and no one can immediately identify which change was made, because directly modifying the prompt in the interface leaves no history or rollback reference.

In this class, we illustrate how to manage prompts as source code within declarative automation bundles and deploy them across different environments. We will sequentially examine the bundle structure, the roles of the validate·deploy·run commands, and the rollback process for issues that arise during operations.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain prompt deployment and rollback by environment.
The roles of bundle validate, deploy, and run stages can be distinguished.

screens.title: Different environments lead to different prompt versions, causing confusion.
screens.lead: When reading about prompt versions differing across three environments, consider what challenges might arise in operations when issues occur.

visual.alt: This shows the development, staging, and production environments each using different prompt versions.
labels: What change has been deployed in the current operation?

paragraphs: The same customer service app has development environment prompts on v7, staging on v5, and production on v6. No one has documented who deployed what to which environment at what time. Even the operational team struggles to immediately state which version is currently running.

The cause is that the prompt was directly modified by a human through the management interface. The modified text does not retain information about who made the change, when it was made, or the reason for the change, and there is no reference point to revert to when issues arise. It is also not guaranteed that the text verified in staging was actually deployed to production.

Prompts are changes that significantly affect the quality of a model's response. They impact services as substantially as code changes, and therefore should be logged, reviewed, and deployed environment-wise, just like code.

This course explains how to manage prompts at the deployment level. Using Databricks' Declarative Automation Bundles as an example, it sequentially covers environment-specific deployments, the roles of validate·deploy·run commands, and how to roll back when issues occur.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Declarative Automation Bundles is the current name of the tool previously known as Databricks Asset Bundles. It is provided as a feature of the Databricks CLI.

screens.title: Should prompts be version-controlled like code?
screens.lead: Think about our team's prompt management approach. You don't need to input an answer; simply selecting a question reveals the instructor's thoughts.

items.prompt: Is there record of who changed the prompt, when, and why?
items.answer: By managing prompts as files in a source repository, commit history becomes the change history. It records who, when, what, and why changed something, along with review records. In contrast, when changes are made directly on the screen, these three elements disappear, and after a problem occurs, you have to manually search to find out who fixed it.

items.prompt: Can we identify which change the prompt that has been deployed came from?
items.answer: The definition of deployment that is in operation must be traceable to a specific commit. If the environment-specific deployment definitions are present in the source code, then the deployed definition in operation corresponds directly to a specific point in the source code. Otherwise, one must directly inspect the environment to determine its current state.

items.prompt: Do you have a baseline to revert to when problems occur?
items.answer: To roll back, you need to know which version was previously stable. The rollback reference point is a commit that has been verified as stable. Without such a reference, you must rely on memory to re-enter the command, and there is no way to verify whether the resulting message truly matches the previous state.

screens.outro: Let us first examine the structure of the tools that enable answering these questions.

screens.title: Bundle and environment-specific deployment structure
screens.lead: Select each tab to read about what the bundle is and how deployment is configured across environments.

visual.alt: One bundle is divided into dev, staging, and prod targets and deployed to respective workspaces.

tabs.label: What is a bundle?
tabs.body: Declarative Automation Bundles are tools that apply software engineering practices—such as source control, code review, testing, and CI/CD—to data and AI projects. They place metadata alongside project source files and define Databricks resources like jobs or pipelines directly in terms of source files. Because these bundles contain end-to-end definitions of the project's structure, testing, and deployment processes, they make it easy to track changes when multiple people are developing together.

tabs.label: The items included in the bundle
tabs.body: This consists of necessary cloud infrastructure and workspace configurations, notebooks containing business logic and source files such as Python, definitions and configurations for resources, unit tests, and integration tests. The resources include Lakeflow Jobs, Lakeflow pipelines, dashboards, Model Serving endpoints, MLflow experiments, and registered models. When prompts are treated as source files or configuration values, prompt versions move alongside code versions.

tabs.label: Split the environment by target
tabs.body:
You can split a bundle into multiple workspaces targeting environments such as dev, staging, or prod. Typically, you first deploy to a personal development workspace for verification, and once verified, you promote it to staging, and then to production. Instead of modifying prompts for each environment, you reuse the same definition by only changing the target, which reduces version differences between environments.

```yaml
bundle:
  name: support_bot

resources:
  jobs:
    answer_job:
      name: support-answer

targets:
  dev:
    workspace:
      host: https://dev.example.com
  prod:
    workspace:
      host: https://prod.example.com
```

tabs.label: Deployment identity root_path
tabs.body: A bundle's unique identity is determined by the root_path property. The default value is ~/.bundle/bundle-name/target-name, so by default, the identity consists of the deployer, bundle name, and target name. If this value is the same across different bundles, deployments interfere with each other. Deployments track created resources by ID rather than by name and store their state in the workspace file system. Therefore, if the bundle name, target, or workspace changes, the connection to previous resources is lost.

screens.outro: Now that we know the structure, let's proceed sequentially to view the three commands for deployment.

screens.title: validate, deploy, run command follow-up
screens.lead: Read the three commands deployed to the target operating system from top to bottom. The description on the right explains what each command does and the symptoms that occur when it is skipped.

data.code:
#1. Verify the settings according to the schema.
databricks bundle validate -t prod

#2. Deploy resources into the operational workspace
databricks bundle deploy -t prod

#3. Execute the deployed job
databricks bundle run answer_job -t prod

#In automations where approval verification is skipped, the option is appended.
databricks bundle deploy -t prod --auto-approve

notes.note: validate verifies whether a bundle can be deployed to Databricks by validating its bundle settings and resource definitions against the corresponding schema. The output includes the bundle name, target, and a summary of the workspace, indicating the identity under which the bundle will be deployed. Skipping this step means that errors or incorrect keys will only be discovered at deployment time.

Deploy puts resources into a workspace. If a resource is not present in the workspace, it is created; if it already exists, it is updated; and if a resource is removed from the bundle, it is deleted from the workspace if it was previously deployed. - If the target is not explicitly specified with -t, the default target declared in the bundle is used, so always explicitly specify the target to prevent unintended deployment to other environments.

run executes a deployed workflow. For example, it runs a specified job. If you only deploy without running, the job will be uploaded but will never be executed. Successful deployment does not imply that the workflow has been verified to function.

--auto-approve skips interactive approvals that might be required during deployment. It can be used in automated environments where human response is not possible, such as in CI pipelines; however, since it disables the safety mechanism of approval, it should be used with caution and carefully considered for specific targets. Additionally, --force-lock is an option that can only be used when a previous deployment was interrupted and a lock remains in place.

screens.outro: Now that I understand the meaning of the command, I will explain a case where a change is rolled back within the operation context.

screens.title: Prompt change rollback affecting only operations
screens.lead: It was acceptable during staging, but quality degraded in production, and the instructor explains this step by step. Please click the next arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Situation assessment
steps.body: The change with the modified prompt passed without issues in staging. However, upon deployment to production, reports have come in indicating a decline in quality for certain questions. The first step should not be to investigate the root cause, but rather to mitigate the impact. Since the responses delivered to users have been continuously deteriorating, we should ensure a path back to the previous stable state.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify what was deployed
steps.body: Check the source history to determine which bundle version has been deployed to the target environment. Since environment-specific definitions are stored in the source, you can identify exactly which commit's definition was deployed to operations. If the changes were previously made directly in the UI, answering this question would have been difficult.

steps.title: Step 2: Determine the rollback reference point
steps.body: Rolls back to the previous commit that was considered stable. The stability of that commit is evidenced by the fact that quality metrics remained stable during its deployment period. Once the baseline is established, no further manual re-entry of the commit message is required, and rollbacks are performed by redeploying with the same definition.

steps.title: Step 3: Redeployment
steps.body: After verifying the commit bundle using databricks bundle validate, execute databricks bundle deploy to the prod target. Deploy updates the resources to match both the bundle definition and the workspace state, so resources are refreshed using the definition prior to the change. Resources missing from the bundle are removed, thus confirming alongside the rollback commit which resources were present.

steps.title: Step 4: Verification and Root Cause Tracking
steps.body: Run the job using Databricks bundle run and verify a successful recovery through quality checks. After recovery, separately track differences between staging and production environments to identify which of the input data, model endpoint, or configuration values changed—this ensures safety when reapplying the same change later. Rollback and root cause analysis are distinct activities, and the order should be rollback first. Finally, evaluate the differences identified in this incident and incorporate them into evaluation datasets or deployment validation items so that similar changes are filtered out before going into production.

screens.outro: A rollback will work only if the environment's identity is separated. Let's examine a misaligned configuration.

screens.title: Misaligned configuration reading: two targets use the same root_path
screens.lead: Read the following settings and symptoms, and select the emphasized sections to verify where the issue lies.

data.text:
targets:
  dev:
    workspace:
      root_path: ~/.bundle/support_bot/shared
  prod:
    workspace:
      root_path: ~/.bundle/support_bot/shared

Symptoms: After changing the prompt in dev and deploying it, production job definition also changes to The operational response has changed..

marks.note: Two targets use the same path. The bundle's identity is determined by root_path, so in this case, dev and prod are treated as a single deployment and share the same resource state. Using the default value of ~/.bundle/bundle_name/target_name creates separate paths for each target.

marks.span: After changing the prompt in dev and deploying it,
marks.note: Deployment tracks resources by ID rather than by name. If resources are grouped under the same identity, the dev deployment will update the production resources. This means the isolation between environments is lost, and rollback plans are also affected.

This is the result of changed responses going to users. To verify, run databricks bundle validate separately in dev and prod environments and compare whether the identity summary path is the same. To fix, remove the two root_path lines and rely on the default value, then redeploy the already-mixed prod environment based on standard commit criteria to align the definition. To prevent the same issue, it's recommended to include in code review items a rule that, whenever a new target is added, the root_path is left to default rather than being explicitly specified.

Symptoms manifest first in the outcome, not in the configuration. The phenomenon of deploying in one environment and then observing a change in another environment is a typical sign of identity overlap. When such a signal appears, immediately place the validation summaries of the two targets side by side for comparison.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the content discussed so far.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: This screen summarizes how prompts are treated on a deployment unit. Please read it slowly and compare it with our team's approach.

paragraphs: Prompts are changes that significantly affect response quality, so they should be treated like code—maintained with version history, reviewed, and deployed across environments. Directly modifying them in the UI does not preserve change history or provide a basis for rollback.

Declarative Automation Bundles define projects using source files and YAML metadata, and deploy to target environments such as dev, staging, and prod. The identity of a bundle is determined by root_path, with a default value that includes both the bundle name and target name.

Deployment proceeds in the following order: first, validate to confirm the settings; then, deploy to push the workspace; finally, run to execute the workflow. Deploy is responsible for the pushing step, while execution is handled by run.

Rollback involves redeploying the definition that was previously in a valid state. First, the reversion is performed, and the root cause is separately traced to differences between staging and production environments. For this, environments must use different root_path values to achieve isolation.

The inspection questions can be grouped into three: where the prompt originated in the operational commit, what the previous stable commit was, and whether the deployment identities of the environments are decoupled. If all three questions can be answered directly, it indicates that the prompt is managed at the deployment level. If any of the questions is difficult to answer, that point should be the first area addressed by our team, and the improvement order can be established based on the rollback explanation in this course.

callout.label: A sentence to remember
callout.text: A prompt is also a deployment unit. You must be able to identify within five minutes which change originated a prompt that has been deployed into production.

checks.q:
After deploying with the following settings in dev, the prod job changed. What is the cause?  

targets:  
  dev:  
    workspace:  
      root_path: ~/.bundle/support_bot/shared  
  prod:  
    workspace:  
      root_path: ~/.bundle/support_bot/shared
options: The host was missing from the prod target and was deployed to dev instead.
Two targets share the same root_path and thus the same deployment identity.
Do not run validate first; the job has been merged as a result.
The run command executes both dev and prod.
checks.explain: The identity of bundles is determined by root_path; if two targets use the same path, they are treated as a single deployment and overwrite each other's resources. If the default value is used, each target gets a separate path.

wrong.0: This is not a host issue; it is because the paths of the two targets are the same.
wrong.2: validate is a verification step and does not involve a merge operation.
wrong.3: run executes only one specified job.

checks.intro: Let's examine the issue with a configuration where two targets use the same path. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Correct. The value determining the identity of the deployment has collided.
checks.incorrectFeedback: You've considered other possibilities. Please double-check how a bundle's identity is determined.

checks.q: Let's look at the bundle command flow in the correct order.
items: validate: Bundle configuration and identity summary verification
deploy -t prod: deploy resources to the target environment workspace
checks.explain: First, verify the settings, specify the target, deploy it, and then execute the deployed workflow.
checks.intro: Consider the correct execution order of bundle commands. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. Confirm, upload, and execute.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Consider which of verification, deployment, or execution serves as a prerequisite for the others.

checks.q: It worked well in staging, but what's the correct way to revert a prompt change that has poor quality in production?
options: After validating the bundle based on the previous stable commit, deploy it to the prod target.
On the operating screen, directly modify the prompt to enter the previous text.
Overwrites the staging target with an operational environment to align the environment.
Maintain the current version until the cause is determined.
checks.explain: Rollback involves redeploying a previous stable definition. The root cause is traced separately based on differences between staging and production environments.

wrong.1: Direct modification is a method that does not preserve a change history or a basis for rollback.
wrong.2: Overwriting when the staging definition's status is unknown can exacerbate confusion.
wrong.3: Since the impact continues to grow, mitigation should be addressed first.

checks.intro: Choose a method to revert prompt issues that occurred only during operation. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Redeploys the original definition along the same path.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This method covers the environment without leaving a trail or providing a way to verify its impact. Consider again what basis you're using to roll back.

glossary.def: This is a project that bundles source files and resource definitions into a single deployment unit alongside YAML metadata.
Target environments for deploying bundles are divided into categories such as dev, staging, and prod.
These are three commands: verify bundle settings, deploy to workspace, and execute the deployed workflow.
The path that defines the deployment identity of a bundle includes the bundle name and target name by default.
This is the process of rolling back a changed version to restore the previous normal definition.

misconceptions.myth: The prompt is merely a document that can be edited in the settings screen.
misconceptions.fact: Prompts are changes that determine response quality. Like code, they require history, reviews, and deployment management.
Deploy is the step of placing resources into a workspace. Running a workflow is referred to as run.

misconceptions.myth: Since dev and prod have different targets, it's acceptable to use the same root_path.
misconceptions.fact: If the root_path is the same, the deployment identity becomes identical, allowing them to interfere with and overwrite each other.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Prompt is also a deployment unit, and the same definition is deployed across environments.
The pipeline reads the name, resources, and target from databricks.yml, and flows through validate, deploy, and run.
Deployment tracks resource states by ID, and identity is determined by root_path.
Rollback means redistributing a previous normal definition.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Can you identify within five minutes where the currently running prompt originated from?
